caption:
What's the best way to close a client on a discovery call?

I'm not a big fan of closing someone on a discovery call.

A discovery call is probably thirty minutes to an hour. If you really want to build trust and rapport and truly understand the pain points of that business, that is what the discovery call is for. To discover if there is an actual fit.

A lot of people do a one call close. I prefer a two call close.

The discovery call is purely there to discover and see synergies. We use the full half an hour to an hour to truly understand the business. What is the business truly like? What are the bottlenecks? What are you struggling with? Where are you truly now, margin wise, profit wise, revenue wise?

Only if we feel we can add value do we schedule a demonstration call and show how we can help.

The other reason is attention span. People only have about thirty minutes. The moment the call goes over thirty to forty minutes they're losing focus, so when you start pitching your services they're not paying as much attention as you want them to.

That's why we like to start a new call fresh a few days later, after we've done our own due diligence and our own bit of research.

So that's why we do a two call close, mainly.

caption:
4 things nobody taught me before I started my business. And not knowing them is exactly why most entrepreneurs struggle.

1. Return on Investment. You spent 100 rupees, how much came back? Agar jawab nahi pata, that’s not a strategy. That’s just spending money and hoping for the best.

2. Cash flow. Profit on paper aur account mein actual paisa, dono alag hain. If money isn’t moving, the business isn’t breathing. Doesn’t matter how good your P&L looks.

3. Customer Acquisition Cost and Lifetime Value. What does it cost to get one customer, and how much will they pay you over time? If what you spend is more than what they give, tum baar baar toot rahe ho.

4. Break-even point. How many sales do you need just to cover every single expense? Yeh nahi pata toh you’re running blind, no matter how busy you feel.

Learn your numbers before your numbers teach you. Because that lesson is always expensive.

caption:
Know who you are before you decide to become an entrepreneur.

Entrepreneurs jump off a cliff and try to build the plane on the way down. 

You have to be able to do that.

In the mid 90s, I was running my own asset management company and we were getting our asses kicked. 

A Goldman colleague comes to visit, sees the operation, gets excited and says he wants to leave and do the same thing.

I said — can I show you something first?

I walked him down the hall and opened a closet. Inside was $850,000 worth of servers and switches.

I said — you see that? That’s my summer house in the Hamptons.

Are you willing to put your summer house in a closet in Midtown Manhattan?

If yes, leave Goldman and start your business. 

If no, shut up and enjoy your career there. There’s absolutely nothing wrong with that.

The big message is simple: Know who you are, know what you’re capable of, know what you actually like doing.

Entrepreneurship is incredible. It’s also brutal. 

Make sure you know which version you’re signing up for.

caption:
Three startups, three different founders, yet remarkably similar lessons emerged from their experiences. Each founder believed they understood what customers wanted, but some important decisions were made without gathering enough direct feedback from the people they were trying to serve. This highlights one of the most important principles of building a successful business: assumptions are not a substitute for listening to customers. Another challenge was how the products were presented, with claims that sometimes made them appear more different or distinctive than customers ultimately experienced. Even small differences between expectations and reality can affect how people perceive a company. Once trust begins to weaken, rebuilding it can take significant time and consistent effort. The broader lesson for entrepreneurs is simple: talk to customers early, test ideas before investing heavily, communicate honestly, and make improvements based on real-world feedback. A great product is not only about having a creative idea; it is also about understanding what people actually need and delivering an experience that matches what you promise.

caption:
This is how you land your first freelancing client:

Honesty, Evidence, Incentive.

1. Honesty: Don’t try to fool anybody, they may not know they’re your first, but they know they’re early adopters. Play into it. Everyone likes an underdog. Now, you don’t want to give them impression that you’ll need a lot of hand holding and that working with you will be difficult, but do give the impression that you’re scrappy and you’re going to wear their jersey and advocate for their success.
2. Evidence: It’s already hard enough to get clients at the start of your career. If you don’t have a portfolio, it’s nearly impossible. Take a week or so and create a few examples of the end result of working with. Remember, a portfolio isn’t the same thing as a resume, it’s not a representation of who you’ve worked with, it’s a demonstration of the solution you’re offering.
3. Incentive: Let’s be real here, if you’re hiring someone who’s untested and unproven in the field, you’re taking a bit of a risk. So de-risk that decision for your potential clients by competing on price (this is one of the only times I offer this advice). Just make sure you don’t offer to do it for free, because that’s bad for the project, and make sure you establish that this is a one time thing for the chance to earn their business, so you can charge for your value on future projects with them.

If a task feels overwhelming, tell yourself you only have to do it for two minutes.
Open the document. Start the email. Write the first sentence.

Your brain is great at thinking, not holding information.

• remember things better
• clear mental clutter
• stop constantly trying to “keep everything in your head”

Take 3 minutes and write tomorrow’s to-do list on paper before bed.

3. Change your environment.
Your environment quietly controls your focus.

If your phone is next to you, your brain is waiting for it to light up.

How to try it today:
Put your phone in another room while you work on one task.
Even 20–30 minutes of distraction-free focus can change your entire day.
